items.title: Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2013
items.q: the concert we’re going to give for example, this Friday, with Dr. Michael Woods

ctx.x: Well last week, timely, there was a couple of Chinese students. I’m not even sure they were teaching assistants, they did an hour program on Chinese popular music. One did something she called Chinese rock & roll. And the other one did, and I wish I had written the word down, there was a term that apparently there’s a popular style that combines almost hip hop, that kind of thing, using traditional Chinese instruments. It was very interesting. And it’s amazing how pervasive Western pop music is now around the…

Well I think perhaps what you’re suggesting is that there is maybe another transformation with the younger generation? I performed with Cui Jian who is the rock icon of China — China’s first rock icon I should say. As a result I had nothing but my name. He expressed © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -7-

the collective feelings of his generation, you know Tiananmen Square was like 1989. And next year will be the 25th anniversary. But Cui Jian expressed the sentiments of those young students at that time, who felt alienated from the cultural revolution. And so the 1980’s was the emergence of rock, but there wasn’t, you know rock represented rebellion, I guess, of the government. And so it was an expression of that but not necessarily — there was a motivation to think of yourself as an artist and trying to develop…
